The Fate of Ocean Plastics: From Surface Mats to Deep-Sea Sinks

We are going to jump right into the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. You have probably seen photos of this massive, floating mat of debris out in the Pacific Ocean—it is roughly twice the area of Texas. But here is the big question: is the surface of the ocean the final resting place for all this plastic?

The answer is no. That floating mat is just a temporary stop. Out in the open ocean, these plastics are subjected to a relentless demolition derby. Mechanical forces from crashing waves smash the pieces together. Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun bakes the plastic, making it brittle. Meanwhile, microbes and chemical processes eat away at the surfaces. All of these forces work together to break large plastic items down into smaller and smaller fragments, eventually forming microplastics and nanoplastics.

When researchers actually scuba dive beneath this giant floating mass, they report seeing something that looks like a mist or a fog in the water. That "mist" is actually a massive concentration of tiny plastic particles starting their long descent from the surface down into the deeper waters.

Scientists have mapped out the concentration of these particles (in the 0.5 to 50 millimeter size range) across thousands of kilometers of the Pacific Ocean, from Honolulu to Rosarito. What they found is a distinct depth profile: the concentration is highest right at the air-water interface, but as you move deeper, you still find plastics. This tells us that particles are actively moving away from the surface and descending through the water column.

Eventually, if these sinking particles reach the seafloor, they settle into the bottom sediments. As more and more sediment deposits on top of them, they become buried. At this point, they are effectively removed from active environmental cycling. In environmental science, we call this a sink—a place where hazardous materials end up and are essentially taken out of the game, no longer posing an immediate threat to surface ecosystems or human exposure.

In environmental science, what exactly makes the deep ocean sediment a "sink" for these degraded plastics?

A sink is a final resting place where materials are removed from active environmental cycling. Once the plastics are buried under layers of sediment on the seafloor, they are essentially taken out of the game and stop interacting with surface ecosystems.

Today, our goal is to figure out exactly how long it takes for these particles to reach that deep-ocean sink, and how their size and density change the rules of the game.

Gravity vs. Brownian Motion at the Nanoscale

Think back to the experiment we looked at on Friday. We dropped different-sized pebbles (roughly 1 mm, 5 mm, and 12 mm) into a graduated cylinder of water. We observed a clear trend: the smaller the pebble, the more slowly it settled to the bottom.

But what happens if we shrink our particle way down? Imagine dropping a 100-nanometer (100 \text{ nm}) plastic particle into that same cylinder. Would it just sink straight downward?

Gravity is always pulling downward on anything with mass. For a macroscopic object like a pebble or a dropped penny, gravity is the undisputed heavyweight champion; the object sinks straight down, maybe fluttering just a tiny bit side-to-side. We call this downward drift gravitational settling.

However, when you shrink down to the nanoscale, the game changes. At this scale, the thermal energy of the water itself becomes a major player. The water molecules are vibrating and constantly body-checking our tiny plastic particle from all sides. This relentless, random jostling is called Brownian motion.

Brownian motion creates random displacements in all directions. It is important to understand that Brownian motion does not cancel out gravity. Gravity is still pulling the particle down. But for very small particles, the random, erratic jumps caused by Brownian motion are so large that they mask the slow downward drift of gravity.

Does the presence of Brownian motion mean that gravity stops acting on nanoscale plastic particles?

Not at all! Gravity is always pulling downward, regardless of the particle’s size. However, at the nanoscale, the random thermal jostling from water molecules is so intense that it overwhelms the slow downward drift, making the particle bounce erratically instead of dropping straight down.

Simulating Particle Trajectories

To really see how these two forces battle it out, we are going to run a computational simulation using Google Colab. Coding can sometimes be intimidating because it relies heavily on exact syntax, but today we are just going to act as the "coaches" calling the plays—we will adjust a few parameters and let the computer do the heavy lifting.

Once you load the notebook, you will see a block of Python code. Look for the section labeled STUDENT PARAMETERS. This is our control panel. Here, we can set the diameters of three different particles (in micrometers, \mu\text{m}), the density of the plastic, the density of the water, and the total observation time in seconds.

For our first run, the code is set to simulate particles that are 0.1 \ \mu\text{m} (which is 100 \text{ nm}), 1 \ \mu\text{m}, and 10 \ \mu\text{m} in diameter. The particle density is set to 1050 \text{ kg/m}^3, which is slightly denser than water (1000 \text{ kg/m}^3). Because they are denser than water, we know gravity wants them to sink.

When we run the simulation, the code calculates the gravitational settling velocity and the Brownian diffusion for each particle, then plots their paths. Let’s look at a set of example trajectories for a 0.2 \ \mu\text{m}, a 2 \ \mu\text{m}, and a 20 \ \mu\text{m} particle.

Coach’s Tip: Always check your axes! The code automatically scales the axes to fit the particle’s movement, so the grids are not identical across the three plots.

Look at the 20 \ \mu\text{m} particle on the far right. It plummets straight down, traveling thousands of micrometers vertically with almost zero horizontal movement. Gravity is totally dominating here.

Now look at the 2 \ \mu\text{m} particle in the middle. It still has a clear downward trend, but it is wiggling side-to-side. Brownian motion is starting to show up on the radar.

Finally, look at the 0.2 \ \mu\text{m} (200 \text{ nm}) particle on the left. This path is wild! It is bouncing everywhere. If you look closely, there are periods where the particle is actually moving upward against gravity. Gravity is still applying a downward drift, but the random thermal kicks from the water molecules are so strong that they overpower the downward pull in the short term.

If we plot the magnitude of displacement versus particle size, we find a crossover point around 1 to 1.5 \ \mu\text{m}. For any particle smaller than that crossover size, Brownian motion is the dominant driver of its movement. In the nanoscale regime, Brownian displacement isn’t just a little bit bigger than gravitational settling—it can be orders of magnitude larger!

The Deep Ocean Journey: Calculating Settling Times

Now let’s apply this to the real world. In Part 2 of our Colab notebook, we use the settling velocities calculated in Part 1 to figure out how long it would take these particles to fall from the surface of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch all the way to the ocean floor—a depth of about 5,000 \text{ meters}.

When we run the numbers for a 10 \ \mu\text{m} particle, the code tells us it takes about 58 years to reach the bottom. That is a long time, but it is within a human lifespan.

What about a 1 \ \mu\text{m} particle? Because it is a factor of 10 smaller, its settling velocity drops dramatically. The calculation shows it would take over 5,000 years to descend those 5,000 \text{ meters}!

And if we look at a 10 \text{ nm} particle? The theoretical settling time stretches into the millions of years.

Reality Check: The Ocean is Not a Bathtub

Before we assume that nanoplastics will float in the water column until the end of time, we need to remember that our Colab simulation is an idealized model. It assumes perfectly still water, isolated spherical particles, and constant properties.

In the actual ocean, things are much messier. We have powerful ocean currents, winds, and thermal fluctuations that sweep particles around. Furthermore, particles don’t stay pristine. Microbes and algae love to attach themselves to floating plastics—a process called biofouling. This biological baggage adds mass and density to the plastic, causing it to sink much faster than our simple math predicts. Tiny plastics also aggregate, clumping together to form larger, heavier particles that fall out of the water column more quickly.

If our theoretical math shows that a 1 \ \mu\text{m} particle takes over 5,000 years to sink, why do we actually find them in the deep-sea sink much sooner?

Our simulation assumes pristine, isolated particles in still water. In the real ocean, microbes and algae attach to the plastics (biofouling), and the particles clump together. This biological baggage adds mass and density, causing the aggregates to sink much faster than the idealized math suggests.

So, while our theoretical calculations show that nanoscale plastics should take millennia to settle, the dynamic, living nature of the ocean ensures they reach the deep-sea sink much faster. Understanding the baseline physics—the tug-of-war between gravity and Brownian motion—gives us the foundation we need to tackle those real-world complexities.
